summary: Iteration 1 confirmed that a skyline-based greedy packer (score 71.76) delivers 2x the packing efficiency of naive strip packing (score 34.59), validating 2D spatial awareness as the dominant mechanism. The skyline packer fell ~4.5 points below the designer's probe (76.21), attributed to fewer candidate widths explored under time pressure. The human reference solution scores ~79, leaving ~7 points of headroom from known techniques not yet implemented.
key_points: Skyline packer scored 71.76 vs strip packer 34.59 — a 2.07x improvement, confirming the core hypothesis that fitting pieces into 2D gaps dominates packing quality.

The 4.5-point gap between the designer probe (76.21) and measured score (71.76) is likely due to time management sensitivity: the width sweep explores fewer candidate rectangle widths on slower hardware, missing better packing configurations.

The human reference solution (78.7) uses four additional techniques not yet tested: lookahead (choosing the best from next N pieces), skyline roughness tiebreaking, column compaction, and multiple piece orderings. These collectively account for ~7 points of potential improvement.
All 70 test cases produced valid output for both arms — transform parameter recovery (reflect→rotate→translate) is correct, which was a known failure mode for other LLM-generated solutions.

Next iteration should focus on: (1) lookahead optimization (expected highest marginal gain — picking globally better placements instead of greedy-next), (2) roughness tiebreaker (smoother skylines leave fewer wasted gaps), and (3) time management tuning to ensure more widths are explored within the 2s budget. An ablation design testing each independently would identify which contributes most.
